title: How to make $100k a month with content in 2026
creator: Tristan Workman (host) with guest Briar Cochran
one_liner: Treat content as measurable marketing: untangle your data, grow the right followers, then follow up.
why_it_matters: Briar runs a short-form agency and gives concrete, testable rules for small accounts like Srijan's: what to measure, how to get ideas, how to avoid ghost followers, and how to plan a week. Tristan adds the sales side: how attention becomes money through follow-up and an email list.

big_idea.statement: A personal brand is the best asset you can build, but only if you treat content like real marketing: one goal, steady 1% improvements, followers who fit, and a path to money.
support: Split every video into hook, format, topic and illustration, and test each part weekly.
How you grow is who your audience becomes; ghost followers stall Instagram reach.
Viral is relative (4–5× your baseline); reach comes from high TAM, storytelling and a conversation goal.
Plan a 4 : 2 : 1 week (reach : mind-blowers : sneak peek) and let stories nurture.
Money comes from DMs, an owned email list, and following up with 'not now' people.

chapters.title: Cold open & Briar's origin story
chapters.summary: The episode opens on a ~46-second hyper-edited teaser of its best lines. Briar's 'gun to my head… Omaha, Des Moines, Fargo' hook comes first, then 'personal brand is the best asset in 2026', the debt story and '1% better every day'. Then the story starts. Briar left a church job in 2023 and spent a year trying to be a creator (podcast, YouTube) without making more than $3K a month. In February 2024 he booked a sales call for Premium Ghostwriting Academy (PGA), and the closer was Tristan. Briar tried to refund his $1,000 deposit, and Tristan won him back with a 'banger' email and a written guarantee: land a client in 8 weeks or Tristan pays for the programme. He landed a $1,000 retainer in week 7.

blocks.text: Personal brand is by far the best asset you can have in 2026.

blocks.title: The gamer who had 'given her no proof'
blocks.text: Briar admits that before this he was playing video games 3–4 hours a day and secretly buying Apex Legends skins ('$500 to get an heirloom') with money his wife Olivia didn't know about. He came into the marriage with about $37,000 of debt and used her savings for the programme. His point: you can't ask why nobody believes in you when you've given them no proof. Self-belief comes first, then you 'stack the chips' until people trust you.

blocks.label: of debt coming into his marriage
blocks.note: Paid off within months of his first $10K month (his account).

blocks.text: Srijan's gaming audience will relate to the Apex-skins confession. Briar's story works because it's specific and a bit embarrassing (secret skins, a $2.50 bag of chips he hid). Use the same honesty in a 'what I spent on gaming vs gym this year' reel.
The '$100k a month' in the title isn't taught as a method. It's a hook the two wrote live later in the episode (1:47:01), reused as the cold open.

chapters.title: Belief, survival mode & keeping the day job
chapters.summary: Briar says nothing felt different until his first 'whale' client. He built self-belief by playing a two-hour motivational-clip YouTube video every morning, then hit $10K a month, cried, and paid off all his debt the next month. They talk about why people quit. A doctor accepts years of med school because the payoff is guaranteed, but entrepreneurs panic without a guarantee and jump between shiny objects ('survival mode'). The fix: get your expenses below your income and build on the side. Tristan adds 'confidence comes from evidence, evidence comes from effort', and warns not to get stuck in the self-help phase without a vehicle to apply it.

left.title: Survival mode
items: No guarantee, so you panic
Two months of one thing, then jump to the next shiny object
Burn the boats with no runway

right.title: Patient builder
items: Expenses below revenue first
Build in your free 2 hours a day and weekends
Keep the job until the side thing proves itself (Dickie Bush kept BlackRock until Ship 30 made double his salary)

blocks.title: The 2-hour motivation video
blocks.text: Every morning Briar played a two-hour compilation from the YouTube channel 'Inspired by Florian' (Goggins, Hormozi, Jocko). Then he landed the first $10K-a-month 'whale' client after a different one bailed a week earlier. Tristan's caution: self-help is fine as fuel, but 'don't get stuck in that self-help phase'. Pick a vehicle (for him, marathons and sales) and act.
Srijan's version: keep the day job or studies, protect one daily slot for content, and track 'effort deposits' (reels posted, scripts written) rather than followers in the first months.

chapters.title: Apprenticeship & cold-DM tactics
chapters.summary: An $8K client changed Briar's life and he quit his job. In January 2025 he took a 50–60-hour-a-week job with marketer Alex Garcia's agency while running his own on the side. It brought about 20% of his income but took 80% of his time, which he calls worth it for the skills. His point: 'the fast track is to go sit underneath someone'. He shares the cold-DM trick that got him that job out of 126 applicants: Instagram Close Friends stories plus a Loom. Tristan got his own job by cold-DMing Dickie Bush on Instagram and 'following up like a madman'. Briar's 2026 tip: DM people on Substack, where nobody else does.

blocks.text: the fast track is to go sit underneath someone

blocks.title: The Close Friends + Loom pitch

items.label: 1. Empty Close Friends
items.text: Remove everyone; add only the people you want to reach (they don't need to follow you).

items.label: 2. Record a Loom
items.text: Pitch yourself with good copywriting.

items.label: 3. Post a story
items.text: Close Friends stories sit 'at the top of their notifications', above follows, DMs and comments.

items.label: 4. Say their name first
items.text: A pattern interrupt: 'this person is literally talking to me'.

items.label: 5. Keep it short
items.text: 'I promise you it's only 3 to 5 minutes.' Then crush the Loom.

blocks.caption: Briar says Alex Garcia had 126 applicants and hired him as 'the most creative one'.

blocks.text: the best cold DM strategy I think in 2026 is DMing people on Substack.

blocks.label: 80% of his time for 20% of his income
blocks.note: His split while apprenticing under Alex Garcia, 'worth it because the skill acquisition'.

blocks.text: For brand collabs: put a Pune supplement brand's or PC store's social team on Close Friends, post a story that says their name, and link a 3-minute Loom showing the exact reel you'd make for them. Or find the founder's Substack and DM there.

chapters.title: Personal brand = the best asset
chapters.summary: March 2025 hit $45K, then Briar overextended: missed deliverables, an editor quit, and he gave every client a free month, so April dropped to about $20K. In May he started his own content, inspired by watching Alex Garcia land clients with one post calling out a brand he wanted to work with. A man on a yacht with a $500M real-estate portfolio told Briar he'd keep his personal brand over the portfolio. Briar's maths: 1% better a day from 300 views gives about 11,400 average views by the end of 2026. He thinks there is a 2–3-year window before AI floods socials. Three blockers stop people: priority, belief and no sacred hour.

blocks.text: If you post on January 1st and you start at 300 views and you get 1% better every day through 2026, okay, just 1%. You will be averaging 11,400 views by December 31st, 2026.

blocks.label: average views after a year of 1% daily improvement
blocks.note: The arithmetic checks out (300 × 1.01³⁶⁵ ≈ 11,330). His add-ons ('top 0.1% of your niche', ~50K followers) are estimates.

items.label: Priority
items.text: Believe it's the most important thing after faith and family. He says he stopped working out for a year to build.

items.label: Belief
items.text: It feels like a gamble, but 'It is as close to a guarantee as any skill there is'.

items.label: Sacred hours
items.text: One fixed hour a day, at the start or end of the day, to record.

items.label: Bonus: start on TikTok
items.text: If you fear school friends on Instagram. Both say that insecurity cost them 'about a year'.

blocks.text: Block off an hour time slot um and record content during that time, one time a day.

blocks.label: before AI floods social and personal-brand 'real estate' dries up

blocks.text: Srijan at ~930 followers: make the sacred hour 7–8 pm after the gym, iPhone 15 on the tripod already set up at the desk. Track average views per week; 1% a day means each week should be ~7% better than the last.

chapters.title: North star, ideation faucets & untangling data
chapters.summary: Briar cites Meta CMO Alex Schultz's book Click Here. A great marketer can state the goal in one sentence and leans into small, steady improvements. People A/B-test emails and ads but treat content as a 'day in the life' hobby. For ideas, he keeps four 'faucets' running: Reddit, a second TikTok account for outliers, his own data turned into buzzwords, and 5 creators inside plus 5 outside his niche. To improve week over week he 'untangles data': every video is split into hook, format, topic and illustration, and each part is tested on its own the next week.

blocks.text: Give me one sentence.

items.label: 1. Reddit
items.text: Your niche's subreddit, sorted by top of the month; paste a thread into ChatGPT and ask what people are talking about.

items.label: 2. A second TikTok account
items.text: Follow only your niche and save videos, but only copy true outliers: 'make sure it's an outlier for them'.

items.label: 3. Your own buzzwords
items.text: Sum up last week's most viral video in one specific buzzword, then make another video on it.

items.label: 4. 5 + 5 creators
items.text: Topics from 5 niche competitors, packaging (formats, camera angles, series) from 5 creators outside your niche.

items.label: 5 creators in your niche
items.text: Take their topics.

items.label: 5 creators outside your niche
items.text: Take their packaging: formats, angles, series.

items.label: The overlap
items.text: Your combo. 'No one knows where you're taking the combos from.'

blocks.title: Untangling data (weekly)

items.label: Hook
items.text: The psychological principle: 'Did I yell at them? Did I give them a timeline?'

items.label: Format
items.text: How it looks: green screen, podcast, whiteboard, day-in-the-life, top-down.

items.label: Topic
items.text: One word or phrase.

items.label: Illustration
items.text: How it was told: metaphor, story, statistic or quote.

items.label: Test each next week
items.text: Keep the parts that still win, drop the ones that don't.

blocks.caption: 'You improve your content by untangling data.'

blocks.title: Buzzword faucet on a gym reel
blocks.before: Last week's hit: 'I ate only canteen food for a week and still hit macros'. Next week: random new idea.
blocks.after: Buzzword: 'budget protein hacks'. Next week: 'Protein from ₹100 at a Pune kirana store', keeping the same hook type and format.
blocks.why: Briar's Roth IRA/Super Bowl → 'creative tax strategies' → Rolls-Royce via Section 8 move, in gym form.

blocks.label: followers a month for his longest client
blocks.note: He says the client who's let him untangle data longest grows fastest.

chapters.title: Follower quality over virality
chapters.summary: Briar calls creator comparison worse than everyday comparison because of survivor bias: the algorithm only shows you the winners. 'That's what an algorithm is.' His bigger point: 'the way you grow and what you grow on is what your audience will always be.' One viral video gives you followers who only know that video; steady growth gives a 'kaleidoscope' following. His thought experiment: would you give a five-minute talk to 130,000 twelve-year-olds in a stadium, or to 10 Fortune 500 CEOs in a small room? Tristan's Ironman series is the cautionary tale: one video hit about a million views and brought him followers who don't fit his sales content.

blocks.text: the way you grow and what you grow on is what your audience will always be.

left.title: 130,000 twelve-year-olds
items: Michigan Stadium, 50-yard line
Huge number
None of them can buy what you sell

right.title: 10 Fortune 500 CEOs
items: A 200 sq ft room
Tiny number
Every one could change your business

items.label: One viral spike
items.text: Followers know you only for that one video ('how to make a medium rare steak').

items.label: Stacked growth
items.text: 1,000 here, 1,000 there, on different videos in your lane.

items.label: Kaleidoscope following
items.text: They know you for several things, so they care when you change topic within your lane.

items.label: Result
items.text: Slower, but higher quality: 'Not all views or followers are created equally'.

blocks.title: Tristan's Ironman series
blocks.text: Tristan documented doing an Ironman with no training: 6 posts in 10 days. A friend pulled him aside mid-run to say he was going viral; one video reached about a million views. But of his roughly 4,000 followers, about 1,200 are 'Iron Man people from Sweden' who won't care about his sales content. Meanwhile a podcast episode with 50 YouTube views brought four DMs saying it changed their life.
Your life will change with just 10,000 quality followers.
If Srijan's one big viral reel was a pure meme with no gym/tech/gaming link, those followers may never watch a PC build. Grow steadily on the three things you'll keep posting about.

chapters.title: Ghost followers & the non-follower test
chapters.summary: Instagram is 'follower first': a new post goes to your followers first as a test batch. If those followers came for something you no longer post about, they scroll past, and the algorithm decides the video is bad and stops showing it to new people. Briar calls them ghost followers. Examples: a Bitcoin creator with 22K followers, 19K of them from modelling days, stuck under 1K views, and 200K accounts getting 2–3K views. His test: check the non-follower view % on your last 5–10 videos. Then weigh how fast you're gaining new followers to decide whether to push on or restart the account.

blocks.text: on Instagram, it's a follower first platform

items.text: You grew followers on a topic you don't post about anymore.
Instagram shows the new post to followers first.
They don't care, so they scroll.
The algorithm reads it as a bad video.
It never reaches non-followers, so views stay stuck at 500–600.

blocks.title: The non-follower test
items: Open your 5–10 most recent videos in Insights
Read the non-follower view % on each
Above ~50% (he also says 60%): 'you're probably fine'
Count mismatched followers: new ones must outnumber them (10K wrong followers → grow to 21K)
Gaining 1 a day? Consider a new account. Gaining hundreds? Push through.

blocks.text: If it's above 50%, you're probably fine.

blocks.label: followers / followers from his old modelling days
blocks.note: A Bitcoin creator Briar worked with who couldn't break ~1K views.

blocks.text: Srijan has ~930 followers, many probably friends and classmates. Briar had 1,500 friends-and-family followers and outgrew them in about three weeks at a couple of hundred new followers a day, so he kept his account. Check the non-follower % on your last 10 reels before changing anything.

chapters.title: What's working (Dec 2025) & how to run a series
chapters.summary: Briar's list of what's working 'right now in December 2025': the clone format (talking to yourself, with 'a couple weeks left' before it's overplayed), series, green screen for beginners instead of mic-in-hand talking heads, Substack (email capture with discovery built in), and, as a 2026 bet, livestreams for educators, which he calls a 'baked-in webinar'. Then they design Tristan's marathon series together. Days can be skipped. Mix in your expertise ('day one of using sales-call tactics to get business owners to run their first marathon'), raise the stakes, and end with 'follow along'. Series give 'the most view to follower ratio'.

blocks.title: What's working (his snapshot, Dec 2025)
items: Clone format: the same person talking to themselves (fading soon)
Series: 'day one of doing X'
Green screen with one image behind you, for beginners
Substack: own the email plus built-in discovery
2026 bet: livestreams for educational creators (two a week)

items.label: Skip days freely

items.label: Give value throughout
items.text: Don't make it all about you.

items.label: Blend in your expertise
items.text: 'Day one of using sales call tactics to get business owners to run their first marathon.'

items.text: A forfeit: 'if I don't, I'm running the marathon twice'.

items.label: CTA

chapters.title: Camera nerves & the six pillars of content
chapters.summary: For nerves, Briar points to The Inner Game of Tennis: do the prep, then let your subconscious run and have fun. His practical trick is to print a photo of your best friend, put it behind the camera and talk to them, then decide later whether to post it. Tristan adds that Tim Ferriss wrote The 4-Hour Workweek as an email to two friends. Briar says caring less about his own content than his clients' is 'very freeing'; sometimes a 10-minute press-play take is his best. He names six pillars of content, including talent management, which he calls 'energy management' when it's your own brand.

blocks.text: print off a picture of your best friend and put them behind the camera

items.label: 1. Strategy
items.text: Top, middle or bottom of funnel? Virality, views or conversions? Rebalance weekly.

items.label: 2. Ideation
items.text: Picking topics.

items.label: 3. Scripting & storyboarding
items.text: Word for word or bullet points.

items.label: 4. Talent management
items.text: How the person performs best: videographer, script, mornings, a phone call, a teleprompter, batching a month, or letting a 'yapper' talk 4–8 minutes.

items.label: 6. Growth tactics
items.text: e.g. trial reels (named, not explained: 'we haven't even got the trial reels').

blocks.text: Energy management is what you call this if it's for yourself.
I have 10 minutes to record. Let me just press play and just see what happens. Sometimes that's my best content.

Srijan's energy management: tape a photo of his funniest friend above the iPhone lens on the tripod, record unhinged gym rants right after training when energy is high, and batch PC explainers on weekends when he's calmer.

chapters.title: Upsides, downsides, saturation & counter-positioning
chapters.summary: Briar says his personal brand means he'll 'never have to worry about money again': $11K in two nights from messaging interested people, and a $10K-a-month retainer from four DMs (his claims). It's also a hedge, since his following could get him any marketing job in Omaha, and Tristan says the same about his sales skill. The downsides: analysis paralysis, shame about missed days (about 10% of his day goes on his relationship with content), and less privacy. On saturation, niches make it 'not real', and maybe three in a thousand people actually do the work. Counter-positioning is 'different positioning', not opposite: you spike into a pocket and grow out of it, like Amazon with books and Vans with skaters.

blocks.text: I literally closed a $10,000 a month retainer off of four DMs.

left.title: Upsides
items: Money on demand from warm DMs ($11K in two nights, his claim)
A career hedge: always employable
Access: reality-TV stars, founders and CEOs DM him; group chats with high-level people

right.title: Downsides
items: Analysis paralysis and perfectionism
Shame when you miss days
Less privacy: recognised in Miami, cornered for free consulting at parties

blocks.text: maybe three out of a thousand people are actually willing to put in the work.
It doesn't mean opposite positioning. It just means different positioning.
You counter position so you can spike into a market and then you grow out of it.

chapters.title: A month of content in two hours & AI for ideation
chapters.summary: Briar's business: a done-for-you short-form agency (target about $150K a month), low-ticket consulting capped around $50K a month, and an Omaha studio where local businesses get a month of content in a couple of hours. The trick is 14 strong topics recorded once, then the same 14 reformatted for the next two weeks (green screen → whiteboard → talking head → podcast style). He only accepts AI scripting for this local tier. For everyone else: 'The way to use AI for content in 2026 has nothing to do with scripting.' Use AI for ideation. His JSON prompt asks for the 'most unique, specific, and observed situation' your ideal viewer has lived. Name a problem nobody has named.

blocks.title: A month of content in one session

items.label: Pick 14 topics
items.text: e.g. copywriting × sales, KPIs, managing a team (bottom of funnel), something funny ('sell to the Grinch'), mental performance.

items.label: Record weeks 1–2
items.text: One format per topic.

items.label: Reformat for weeks 3–4
items.text: Same 14 topics, new formats: green screen → whiteboard → talking head → podcast.

items.label: Script or yap
items.text: AI scripting prompts for locals, or let a good 'yapper' talk 4–8 minutes and build the script in the edit.

blocks.caption: His caveat: the feedback loop is worse ('You want feedback loop daily if you can'). It's an '8 out of 10 service' for local businesses.

blocks.title: The ideation prompt's three filters

items.label: Unique
items.text: Not generic ('not just planting my carrots').

items.label: Specific
items.text: Not 'watering stuff'.

items.label: Observed

blocks.text: Finally, someone's talking about follower quality.

chapters.title: Polarise without lying & brand = title + emotion
chapters.summary: How to make polarising content: take a hard stance on something you actually believe and don't say things just to anger people. Rage bait with no belief behind it 'has no personal brand value'. 'We don't want to live in the gray.' Briar's example take is 'building in public is the worst content strategy'. He keeps the nuance for private consulting. People who disagree argue in the comments, which drives reach, and they're people he wouldn't want as clients anyway. Tristan adds that a shared enemy is one of the best copywriting principles. Then a definition: a personal brand is a title people would give you plus one emotion attached to it (Nike = hard work; New Balance = style).

blocks.title: Where a take should sit

items.label: Believe it + hard stance
items.text: The goal: a tribe agrees, the other side argues in the comments ('building in public is the worst content strategy').

items.label: Believe it + nuanced
items.text: Keep for private consulting or long form, not for reels.

items.label: Don't believe it + hard stance
items.text: Rage bait: 'it makes them look like an idiot', no fandom.

items.label: Don't believe it + nuanced
items.text: Grey and forgettable (our extrapolation; he only says avoid the grey).

blocks.caption: He says he holds his hard stances about 90% of the time.

blocks.text: We don't want to live in the gray.
can someone give you a title and can they add just one emotion to it?

left.title: Nike
items: Title: shoe company
Emotion: 'just do it', hard work, 'taking over the world'

right.title: New Balance
items: Title: shoe company
Emotion: style. 'Made for the dad in Ohio and the supermodel in London'

blocks.text: Srijan's tombstone test: title = 'the gym + PC guy from Pune'; emotion = chaos/laughter (unhinged). A green/red take he actually believes, e.g. 'Prebuilt gaming PCs are a scam for anyone who can follow a YouTube video', will fill the comments with people who disagree.

chapters.title: Live virality workshop: the Omaha hook
chapters.summary: Tristan asks Briar to engineer a viral clip live, and Briar's recipe has three parts: high TAM (go 'one layer higher'), storytelling with curiosity loops, and a conversation goal (comments, sends or saves, since 'you can't usually hit both'). Being unique and having a great hook sit on top, and he calls those the hardest to teach. He explains 'comment farms' and why you re-open a curiosity loop about 15 seconds in. Then they script the Omaha / Des Moines / Fargo hook that became the episode's cold open. He also redefines viral as relative: 'viral for you' is 4–5× your own baseline.

items.label: High TAM
items.text: Speak to as many people as possible: 'one layer higher'.

items.label: Storytelling
items.text: Curiosity at the start, more loops as you go, metaphors, stats, unique and specific.

items.label: Conversation goal
items.text: Pick comments, sends or saves: usually one or two.

items.label: Unique + great hook
items.text: 'Those two things are harder to teach.'

items.label: = A viral video
items.text: For top-of-funnel content only.

blocks.title: The TAM ladder

items.label: Ambition
items.text: 'How many ambitious people are there in the world?' He aims for billions on top-of-funnel posts.

chapters.title: The weekly content pie (4 : 2 : 1 + stories)
chapters.summary: For a coach who wants to double a following of potential clients, Briar's weekly pie is 4 top-of-funnel, 2 middle-of-funnel and 1 bottom-of-funnel posts. Top-of-funnel posts go wide (high TAM) but must keep a through-line to what you sell. Posting about the Sydney Sweeney jeans campaign when you teach real estate is his example of no through-line. Middle-of-funnel posts should 'blow their mind' with real blueprints, and he says don't make things up. Bottom of funnel shows what you sell without pitching: a client's journey told with 'on our next consulting call we did…' (Tristan names this the 'sneak peek inside'). Stories sell hard twice a week and otherwise show life. 'Stories are not a discovery mechanism.'

items.label: 4 × Top of funnel
items.text: High TAM with a through-line. Airbnb-coach examples: '5 cities nobody's talking about for 2026', 'how much my 5 Airbnbs made', '9 travel hacks', 'Justin Bieber recorded his album at this Airbnb'.

items.label: 2 × Middle of funnel

items.label: 1 × Bottom of funnel

chapters.title: Paid ads, fast growers & answering in hooks
chapters.summary: Tristan says two businesses he worked in made about $5M and $4M in 2.5 years, with roughly 90% of the traffic organic (his claim). Briar warns that ads without an organic presence convert poorly (closers close '10 15% higher' when buyers can see your content), and ad-only exposure makes people auto-scroll your organic posts (an account with 446K followers getting 1–2K views). 'Follower ads are terrible': paid followers skip the first 3 seconds and tank your hook rate. Fast growers analyse data, stay on one line for a year or more, and don't miss days: never skip on TikTok, skip at most one bad day on Instagram, and keep a 14–15-video bank. Tristan notes Briar answers every question with a hook, which is how guests help a podcast grow 'through your clips'.

Briar's way of answering in hooks: pause, form one clear sentence, then 'It's just like two or three principles and then move on.' Tristan: even a cringey 'here's three things' beats no framework at all.

chapters.title: Tristan's $1M month & the PGA funnel
chapters.summary: Tristan tells how PGA's writing businesses hit $1M in November 2024. On the last day, flying to Amsterdam, they were six enrolments short. He wrote a 'quick question (time-sensitive)' email with honest selfish interest, a $500-a-month payment plan, a deadline and a refund-plus-lunch guarantee. Then he texted leads 'maniacally' from the plane and closed the last one at 11:55 pm. His 'or die' / 'flu game' mindset comes from 100-mile races: what would you do if your family's life depended on the number? He then breaks down how Ship 30 and PGA grew: two founders with their own audiences, daily threads, unscalable service early on, bottleneck analysis, an email list, spin-off products, and a 0.2% refund rate.

blocks.title: The last-day email
blocks.text: Subject: 'quick question (time-sensitive)', all lowercase. Body: you've been talking with us for months; maybe it's time, money or fear; here's my selfish interest (a personal goal and a $1,000 bonus for Christmas presents); I'm certain you'll succeed if you follow the plan; $500 a month over 14 months, today only; I'll work with you free if you don't land a client in 8 weeks. PS: if it's the worst decision you ever made, 'I'll just refund you and I'll buy you lunch'. Then mass texts from 30,000 ft. Six enrolments landed, the last at 11:55 pm Eastern, and the month closed above $1M.
the fourth week of the month is always like double and the last day of the month is always like three or four times normal.

chapters.title: Follow-up: the counter-position & the maths
chapters.summary: Tristan's 2026 plan: he paid for about 30 founders and salespeople to run the Austin Marathon and wants to document it. His content counter-position: while sales creators post objection-handling videos, he'll teach 'the art of follow-up', and Briar suggests a weekly video on it. There are 'now' and 'not now' people, and a 'not now' person can become a 'now' person with nurture. 'Content is like a mini followup in itself', Briar adds. Tristan manages reps with results → pipeline → activity, and adds follow-up closes as the forgotten fourth funnel lever. Together they model 100K views → $175K a month, rising to $536K with better organic plus a founder 'quick question' re-engagement email (their example, not real results).

chapters.title: Email list, mentorship & the long game
chapters.summary: CTA cadence: stories sell twice a week, plus one weekly bottom-of-funnel CTA to a lead magnet (a 5-day email course) attached to a series so it 'makes sense' ('comment DATA'). Why own a list: a follower sees a given Instagram video under 50% of the time, while email gets close to 100% notification. 'You own it.' Tristan says half of PGA's booked calls come from its email list. Briar calls mentorship 'just another word for speed': work for them or pay them, then ask short, specific questions. Tristan adds the 'ignorance tax' and his claim that only about 8% of course buyers succeed. They close on picking a vehicle and acting ('Your vehicle will find you through action'), doing hard things as proof, being useful to others, and playing an infinite game.

production.detail: A ~46 s hyper-edited teaser of the single most contrarian soundbite: black screen with glowing 'If I have to make $100,000/MONTH in…', then the guest's 'gun to my head… Omaha, Nebraska; Des Moines, Iowa; Fargo, North Dakota. Why?'. Ends on a metallic thud and a hard cut to black.

Teaser: shots 0.8–1.8 s, aggressive jump cuts, 10–15% push-ins and push-outs, screen flashes, speed ramps synced to percussive hits. Body: wide multi-cam master with long uncut conversational takes; the pattern interrupts are the live demos (hook workshop ~1:36–1:51, content pie ~1:51, follow-up maths ~2:40).
Teaser only: drone shots of Omaha, Des Moines and Fargo with location stamps. Body: minimal, plus on-screen emails Tristan references.
Teaser: heavy bass-driven cinematic riser/beat; impacts and bass drops on key text pops ('$100,000/MONTH', 'WHY'); whooshes on push-ins and text slide-ins. Body: no music bed, dialogue only.

Teaser pairs a brush script ('If I have to make') with a heavy extruded condensed sans ('$100,000/MONTH'), with outer glow, chromatic aberration and scale pop-ins on cubic-bezier easing. Palette red #FF0033, cyan #00CCFF, white, charcoal. Custom animated text, not auto-captions.

Two people in ¾ profile, medium-wide; high-key soft three-point light with a rim; wood-slat acoustic panels, a faux-boxwood wall with a monitor, green velvet armchairs, plants; SM7B-style dynamic mics.
Teaser: high-contrast graphic look. Body: warm, natural and balanced, saturated greens against warm skin.
A long, slow podcast is sold by a short, hyper-edited teaser of its most contrarian line, and that line was scripted live inside the episode.

takeaways.text: Untangle every video into hook, format, topic and illustration; test one variable at a time next week.
Ideation faucets: niche subreddit top-of-month, a second TikTok for outliers, last week's winner as a buzzword.
Only copy true outliers: compare a video with that creator's own average.
Topics from 5 niche creators, packaging from 5 outside creators.
Use AI for ideation, not scripting.

For reach, go one layer higher on TAM; keep a through-line.

Don't overthink hooks: say something crazy and get into it.
Polarise only on what you believe: green or red, never grey.

Series: skip days freely, blend in expertise, raise the stakes, 'follow along'.

One sacred hour a day to record.

1% better a day compounds (300 → ~11,400 average views in a year).

Weekly pie: 4 top, 2 middle ('blow their mind'), 1 bottom ('sneak peek inside').
Stories sell twice a week and nurture; they don't bring discovery.
Follower ads and ad-only exposure hurt organic reach.
One weekly lead-magnet CTA tied to a series; own the email list.

Close Friends story + Loom, or Substack DMs, to reach anyone.

quiz.q: Who is the host and who is the guest?
quiz.a: Tristan Workman hosts; Briar Cochran (short-form content agency, Omaha) is the guest.

quiz.q: What four parts does Briar split every video into?

quiz.a: Reddit (top of the month), a second TikTok account for outliers, your own data as buzzwords, and 5 in-niche + 5 out-of-niche creators.

quiz.q: When is a 20K-view video not an outlier?
quiz.a: When that creator averages more, e.g. 100K.

quiz.q: What are ghost followers and how do you check for them?
quiz.a: Followers who no longer care about your content and stall reach because Instagram tests posts on followers first. Check the non-follower view % on your last 5–10 videos; above ~50% is probably fine.

quiz.q: What three ingredients make Briar's virality recipe, and which two are hardest to teach?
quiz.a: High TAM, storytelling and a conversation goal; being unique and the hook are hardest to teach.

quiz.q: Why re-open a curiosity loop around 15 seconds in?
quiz.a: People who 'got the point' by then leave; a new loop keeps watch time up.
4 top-of-funnel high-TAM posts with a through-line, 2 middle-of-funnel 'blow their mind' posts, 1 bottom-of-funnel 'sneak peek inside'.
Paid followers are half-interested, skip the first 3 seconds, and drag down hook rate and watch time, so the algorithm stops pushing your posts.
Different positioning, not opposite: spike into a pocket (Amazon with books, Vans with skaters), then grow out.

quiz.q: What's in the founder 'quick question' email?
quiz.a: A lowercase 'quick question' subject; as founder, note the call with the rep; restate their pain and goal; ask if the rep showed up and answered everything and why they didn't move forward; PS with a similar client's win.

quiz.q: Where does Briar say AI belongs in content?
quiz.a: Ideation, not scripting (AI scripting only for his local-business tier).

quiz.q: Why own an email list, according to Briar?
quiz.a: A follower sees a given Instagram video well under half the time, but email gets ~100% notification, and you own it.

try_it.title: Untangle last week's best reel
steps: Pick your most-viewed reel from the last 7 days.
Write its hook principle, format, topic (one word) and illustration (story / stat / metaphor / quote).
Next week make 4 reels, each changing only one of the four.
Keep what still wins; log it in a simple sheet every Sunday.

try_it.title: Ghost-follower check
steps: Open Insights on your last 10 reels.
Note the non-follower view % on each and average them.
Above ~50%: keep going. Well below: list which old reels brought followers who don't fit gym/tech/gaming.
Plan only on-line content for a month and recheck.

try_it.title: The Omaha hook, gym edition
steps: Strong statement: 'If you train at a fancy AC gym, you don't actually care about gains.'
One-line reason: 'You're there for the mirrors and the protein café.'
Re-hook at ~15 s: 'Gun to my head, 90 days to get jacked? I'm picking a ₹500-a-month Pune akhada. Why?'
Payoff + a comment-farm closer (a deliberately odd detail in the frame, like a pressure cooker on the bench).

try_it.title: A series with stakes
steps: 'Day 1 of building a gaming PC with only OLX parts.'
Blend in expertise: one real tip per day (PSU wattage, thermal paste).
Stakes: 'If it doesn't boot by day 10, I sell my GPU.'
End every part with 'follow along'; post days 1, 2, 4, 7, 10 so people can binge.

try_it.title: 5 + 5 creator combo
steps: Save 5 Indian gaming creators; list their top topics this month.
Save 5 creators outside gaming (cooking, fashion, finance) with a format you love.
Combine one gaming topic with one outside format (e.g. a 'cooking show' recipe for the perfect BGMI loadout).
Post it and compare it with your baseline (viral for you = 4–5×).

try_it.title: Weekly 4 : 2 : 1 plan
steps: Write 4 wide reach ideas that still connect to gym/tech/gaming.
Write 2 mind-blowers with real screens or numbers (your split, your PC part prices).
Write 1 sneak-peek post (a friend's progress on your plan, or a DM Q&A).
Use stories for life on most days and a direct ask on two days.
